In the name of God, the Merciful, the Compassionate. Praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds, and I pray for blessing and peace upon him who was sent as a mercy to the worlds, and upon his family and his Companions and whoever is guided by his guidance and follows his practice until the Day of Judgement. Peace be upon you, and the mercy of God and His blessings.

To proceed: God, mighty and majestic, created this earth and what is in it for the benefit of the children of Adam, and prepared for them in it the means of living, and made it a container for the living and the dead, and gathered in it of the kinds of provision and of the kinds of what humanity needs such as cannot be exhausted until humanity is exhausted. No soul will die until it has completed its provision. For this reason it was among the wonders of God's kindness, glorified and exalted, that when He spread humanity over this earth and knew the vast numbers of humanity which increase with time and multiply, He created death, so as to help by it in reducing these numbers, so that the earth might be broad enough for its people. Had God not created death, the earth would have filled with the children of Adam, and they would have taken what is in it of good things and exhausted what is in it of resources, and would not by that have been able to share in living in this worldly life.

But God created death for this far-reaching wisdom. Then, had He informed them of death and not created hope for them, the earth would have become straitened for them for all its breadth — even if it were broad and its provisions many — because whoever knows that death lies behind him watching for him cannot find life pleasant. But He created hope for them, so that a person does not cease to hope for life even while he is in his death throes and in the departure of the soul: he hopes to live, and so he earns and offers something for those who will live on this earth after him. God, glorified and exalted, made people of three kinds. The first kind cannot earn their provisions and are not able to do so; they are incapacitated, either with a complete incapacity or with a partial one, so that they do not have the capacities with which to bear the earning of their provisions and their needs. The second kind: God Most High made equal what He gave them of capacities and their needs, so that they have such capacities as cover their needs and add nothing to them. The third kind: God gave him more capacities than his needs, so that he produces for others. And God, glorified and exalted, by His arrangement, made this class in need of the other classes, unable to lord it over them; and by hope He made him think in a way in which he lives for centuries upon centuries. For the producer does not produce for his own lifetime only; were that so, those innovators would not have produced who brought innovations that had consequences after them in the history of humanity, because they would only be producing according to their own need. But by God's arrangement, and by this hope which He created, these men think for an unbounded time, and hence they produce an unceasing production.

Then God, glorified and exalted, guaranteed four things to Adam in the Garden, which are the roots of the benefits. He said, exalted is He: {Indeed it is yours that you shall not go hungry in it nor be naked, and that you shall not thirst in it nor be exposed to the sun} (Sūrat Ṭāhā 20:118–119). These four things are the necessities of human beings. First: "it is yours that you shall not go hungry in it" — this meets the necessity of food. Then He said: "nor be naked" — this meets the necessity of clothing. Then He said: "and that you shall not thirst in it" — this meets the necessity of drink. Then He said: "nor be exposed to the sun" — that is, you shall not be exposed to the sun — and this meets the necessity of shelter. These four are the mother-necessities of human beings absolutely. Then there was added to them, after Adam's descent to this earth and his going out of the Garden, he and Eve, after their nakedness had become apparent to them and they began to stitch over themselves from the leaves of the Garden — there was added to them the human being's need for his own kind, so that this might be a cause of the continuance of offspring; and so it was a fifth necessity, not guaranteed in the Garden but rather for the people of the earth.

Beyond these necessities, what follows divides into two kinds: into needs (ḥājiyyāt) and into refinements (taḥsīniyyāt), or complements (takmīliyyāt); and human beings need all of that. But their need for the necessities is greater than their need for the needs, and their need for the needs is greater than their need for the complements. Hence God, glorified and exalted, made the necessities easy and prepared in all times. From the time of Adam to this age of ours, the air — the oxygen that people breathe above the earth — is made easy and simple. Had it been like the precious minerals that humanity needs, it would have required capacity and expenditure and effort, and a great number of people would die who are unable to reach that capacity or that effort. But God knew everyone's need of it, so He made it easy for them above the earth. Likewise the need for water: God made upon the earth expanses of water sufficient to give people drink, and made in the deserts layers of ground that hold the waters which enter the hollows of the earth and filter them; and He made the mountains have a capacity for filtering the waters and bringing out their salts and bringing out what is in them of harmful things, so that they may be ready for humanity to drink. And likewise He caused to grow upon this earth such kinds of trees and fruits and good things as made humanity, and the other animals that live on this earth, able to be self-sufficient by that even before manufacture and before inventions. These necessities did not need much thought nor much invention: from the time humanity began, it has known how to build from stones a house that shelters it from heat and cold, and it has known how to till the earth and sow in it, and it has known how to obtain water and draw it out of the earth. These are necessities that God made easy.

There is no doubt that many of you will wonder when you learn that water is classified in the genus of minerals; it is like the other precious minerals, except that it has never been found in a place in the depths of the earth but that humanity has discovered it in the past, while the other minerals surround it on every side and no one looks at them or discovers them. Many of our fathers and forebears used to discover waters in the depths of the earth and know the places where they are, while kinds of precious minerals surrounded these waters without their becoming aware of them or being able to reach them. Likewise, when God, glorified and exalted, knew people's need for meat and milk and their products, He sent down eight pairs of grazing livestock from the Garden, and these were the origins of livestock on this earth. Then He sent down iron, in which there is great force and benefits for people, and it was the origin of all the crafts. And He taught Adam agriculture, and that was the origin of all tillage and cultivation. So these things were sufficient to guarantee survival and living on the surface of this earth. God has, of the other planets in our solar system and in others, many times the earth, upon which He did not place these provisions and in which He did not place these blessings.

For this reason God, glorified and exalted, said: {So He decreed them seven heavens in two days, and revealed in every heaven its command. And We adorned the lowest heaven with lamps, and as a protection. That is the determining of the Mighty, the All-Knowing} (Sūrat Fuṣṣilat 41:12), after His words: {Say: do you indeed disbelieve in the One who created the earth in two days, and set up rivals to Him? That is the Lord of the worlds. And He placed in it firm mountains above it, and blessed it, and determined in it its sustenance, in four days, alike for those who ask} (Sūrat Fuṣṣilat 41:9–10). Notice that He mentioned four kinds of creation in the lower world, matched by four kinds of creation in the upper world — and that is for the balance between these two roofs, the lower roof and the covering roof. He made between them a wondrous and marvellous balance. He said: {Say: do you indeed disbelieve in the One who created the earth in two days, and set up rivals to Him? That is the Lord of the worlds} — this is the creation of the crust of the earth and what is in it. Then He said: {And He placed in it firm mountains above it} — and these are the mountains, and in them are most remarkable benefits for humanity. They are what prevents the earth from swaying with you, and they are what people take as signs and are guided by, and they are what stores the waters and filters them, and they are what contains the precious minerals in their hearts; and they are likewise a means of holding out against an enemy and of hiding from the eyes of predatory animals. All of that is among the benefits of these mountains. Then He said after this: {And blessed it} — and this blessing that is in the earth is what brought forth its fruits and caused its trees to grow and placed in it the precious minerals and the good fruits. {And determined in it its sustenance, in four days} — and this is the fourth of the kinds of creation in the lower world: that He determined in it its sustenance. So He prepared in every land such sustenance as its inhabitants need. The deserts, whose inhabitants are few, have few fruits and crops in them; and the lands crowded with inhabitants have many rivers in them and many trees and many crops. This is the arrangement of the Mighty, the All-Knowing, who knows the places suitable for humanity to settle and draws to them the souls that suit that land. To some environments of intense heat He draws peoples suited to this environment, and to some environments of intense cold He draws other peoples suited to that environment; and between this and that are various places, and to each environment He draws the kinds of human beings suited to it. And that has an effect even on their characters and their natures and their colours and their languages.

For this reason God Most High said: {And among His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth and the difference of your tongues and your colours} (Sūrat al-Rūm 30:22). So He linked the difference of tongues and colours with the creation of the heavens and the earth, which indicates that the difference of tongues and colours is affected by environments and by the pattern of living and by the manner of dwelling. For this reason you see the change of colours over the generations because of the change of dwelling and environment and livelihood: the colours change and the tongues change — whether that be by complete change, as happens in the passage from one language to another. The original languages are a limited set; Ibn ʿAbbas said they are seventy-five languages, but there branched out from them such languages as only God knows. The Indian subcontinent alone has four hundred and eighty languages spoken by the Indians — four hundred and eighty languages in a limited region in a single state. Likewise in the European countries, which are among the narrowest and most crowded of countries, there is a great number of divergent languages and dialects: in France alone there are three dialects of the French language, and in England four divergent dialects, and so on. And this is part of the civilisational development that entails the complete change of languages. The Semitic languages, for example, are divergent: the difference between Hebrew and Arabic is very clear, and likewise the difference between Persian and Turkish, for example. And the influence of some languages upon others is clear, because of the mixing of environments, such as the influence of Arabic upon Urdu and Turkish, and the influence of Arabic upon Persian as well.

Then these languages have a remarkable slow movement that proceeds with time. If the people of any language took an old dictionary that was in circulation a thousand years ago, and wanted to communicate among themselves by the words in it, they would find that very hard and difficult. Hence the poems of the English of a hundred years ago are not understood by schoolchildren today in their own country, because the language has developed; and with the development of the figures of speech and the variety of significations the meanings of the words differ, and so those poems are not understood. And the most static of languages is the Arabic language: the children of the Arabs to this day, if one of them hears the words of Imruʾ al-Qays, "Halt, you two, and let us weep at the memory of a beloved and a dwelling," understands the meaning of this hemistich by his native instinct — and even if he does not understand the meaning of the whole construction, he understands the words. This line was said at least a hundred years before the birth of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him). And because of the static character of the Arabic language, God, glorified and exalted, chose it for His Book, the Qur'an, by which the proof is established against whoever it reaches. Had the Qur'an been sent down in a language other than Arabic, it would no longer be fit for understanding today, and would have needed many commentaries in every age. But in view of the static character of this language, it was chosen to be the language of the Qur'an, for its fixity and the rarity of change in its significations.

Then these four kinds of created things in the earth God, glorified and exalted, paired with four kinds of created things in the upper world, where He said: {Then He turned to the heaven while it was smoke, and said to it and to the earth: come, willingly or unwillingly. They said: we come willingly. So He decreed them seven heavens in two days} (Sūrat Fuṣṣilat 41:11–12). And this corresponds to His words: {Say: do you indeed disbelieve in the One who created the earth in two days?} So these seven heavens in the upper world are matched by the seven earths in the lower world. {And revealed in every heaven its command} — and this corresponds to His words: {And blessed it}. And this command that is in the heaven is veiled from us and we do not know it, because it is not prepared for us; the heaven is not prepared to be inhabited by human beings, and for this reason they have not discovered what corresponds to this blessing which they discover in the earth. {And revealed in every heaven its command} — then He said: {And We adorned the lowest heaven with lamps} — and these correspond to the mountains in the earth in His words: {And He placed in it firm mountains above it}; for the stars in the heaven are in the position of the mountains in the earth. Then He said: {And We adorned the lowest heaven with lamps, and as a protection. That is the determining of the Mighty, the All-Knowing} — and this protection is what corresponds to His words: {And determined in it its sustenance}. So this protection that is in the heaven corresponds to the sustenance that is in the earth; and hence the angels are made independent of provisions by the protection. They are honoured servants who do not disobey God in what He commands them and who do what they are commanded; and by God's protection of them they are made independent of provisions, so that they are not like the people of the earth and its inhabitants, who need provisions of this kind.

It was among the arrangement of God, glorified and exalted, that these good things veiled within the earth — and especially those of them that relate to the needs and the complements — cannot be discovered in a single age, nor extracted in it; for had they been extracted in it, people's requirements would have been exhausted, while humanity keeps expanding and its requirements keep increasing. So God Most High made the discovery of these good things gradual. Here in these lands of ours we discovered the mineral of iron, and people lived for a time on this mineral; and after it other minerals are discovered, so that there may be discovered minerals easier and more accessible than it, such as oil, for example, or other minerals that people need. And so it is in all countries; and this is the arrangement of the Mighty, the All-Knowing.

Among His arrangement, glorified and exalted, is that He made these provisions in this earth common property, and did not make them the individual property of their discoverer but made them for humanity. So He made the wealth that is in the earth the property of God, glorified and exalted, and human beings are only stewards over it. This requires of them that they not squander it and not be extravagant with it, and that they not shut it off for themselves and not prevent others from benefiting from it — because it is God's wealth, and the human being in it is only a steward. He is in the position of an agent who awaits dismissal at every moment; and his dismissal is either by death, so that he moves on and leaves behind what he had, as He said, exalted is He: {And you have come to Us as individuals, as We created you the first time, and you have left behind you what We bestowed upon you; and We do not see with you your intercessors whom you claimed were partners among you. The bond between you has been cut, and what you used to claim has strayed from you} (Sūrat al-Anʿām 6:94) — or by an interdiction laid upon his hands, so that he cannot dispose of his wealth; or by his being overpowered and imprisoned; or by an illness that prevents him from disposing; or by the diminishing of his mind through old age and senility; or by other kinds of dismissal by which God dismisses whom He wills from disposing of the wealth He placed under his hand.

God, glorified and exalted, has set out for us that this wealth which He placed in this earth is His property, glorified and exalted, and is not our property, and that He has only made us stewards over it. He said, exalted is He: {And spend from that over which He has made you stewards} (Sūrat al-Ḥadīd 57:7). That is why, when He addressed the angels with His words: {Indeed I am placing on the earth a steward} (Sūrat al-Baqarah 2:30) — that is, a steward over what is in the earth of the kinds of good things and properties. And He set out that He created this for us in His words:

{He created for you all that is in the earth} (Sūrat al-Baqarah 2:29). And this divides into three kinds: into what was created for benefit, what was created for the taking of a lesson, and what was created as a test. What was created for benefit is such as the kinds of provision in this earth from which people derive benefit. What was created for the taking of a lesson is such as what is in this earth that neither benefits nor harms, but which we see and take a lesson from — such as the kinds of non-venomous and non-harmful insects which we find when we dig metres into the earth: we find in it kinds of worms and other kinds of animals that live within the earth; and a person takes a lesson from them and says: from where does air come to them, and who brings them water, and how do they live? And likewise what we see in the deserts of kinds of gazelles and wild beasts and others: a person says, from where does water come to them, and how do they live, and what is their food? And he recalls the words of God Most High: {And there is no creature on the earth but that its provision is upon God, and He knows its dwelling-place and its place of deposit; all is in a clear record} (Sūrat Hūd 11:6). And then a person will be one who takes a lesson and profits from these animals and from the other kinds of what God created in the earth; for God created nothing in vain. Everything in the earth is for a far-reaching wisdom: {And We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in play} (Sūrat al-Anbiyāʾ 21:16). The third kind is what was created as a test, and it is what God sets over the human being of kinds of germs and microbes and kinds of deadly epidemics — and even the kinds of deadly weapons, for which He makes available someone who discovers them and exploits them; for these were created as a test for humanity. A person falls ill and is struck by calamities and dies, and all of that is a test for him: {He who created death and life to test you, which of you is best in deed} (Sūrat al-Mulk 67:2). All of them are among the remarkable tests and trials.

As for these provisions: if we know that they are owned by God, glorified and exalted, then it is upon us not to squander them, and to be just in distributing them, and not to monopolise them, and not to hoard them for ourselves to the exclusion of others. These are the foundations upon which the Islamic economy rests. For every civilisational project, whatever it may be, must show its view of the sensitive subjects that people live with; and among the sensitive subjects that people live with is the subject of the economy. And the Islamic view of the whole world is an integrated civilisational project, and for that reason it has been necessary to set out its various aspects, and especially to speak on the sensitive subjects, such as the subject of humanity's economy. Therefore there must appear for the Muslims a prominent view and an objective outlook regarding this economy, and regarding the earning of it, and regarding its distribution.

For the resources that are in the earth and the benefit that is in it are, as we have mentioned, the property of all: the believer and the unbeliever enter into it. So it is not for the believer to monopolise the good things and deny them to the unbeliever. For this reason the scholars have stated explicitly that it is not permissible for him, if he finds of water only what suffices for his ablution or for the drink of an unbeliever, or a biting dog, or an animal that is not protected — it is not lawful for him to kill it by thirst and perform ablution with that water. Rather he must either give it to drink and perform dry ablution (tayammum), or kill it and perform ablution with the water after killing it; and that is because it shares in this water and has a right in it. This includes all animals — so much so that it is established in the two Ṣaḥīḥs from the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) that a prostitute of the Jews had her sin forgiven her by God because of a dog she passed by at a well, panting and eating the moist earth from thirst; so she went down and took off her boot and scooped water with it and held it in her mouth until she climbed up, and gave the dog to drink — and God forgave her. And it is likewise established from the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) that he said: "A woman entered the Fire because of a cat she tied up: she neither fed it nor let it go to eat from the creatures of the earth." So this entails the sharing of all kinds of animals in these provisions which God created in this earth, and the benefiting of all from them.

Hence, among people there are those who are keys to good and locks against evil; and among them — we ask God for safety and well-being — are those who are locks against good and keys to evil. Those who are keys to good open doors to kinds of provision and benefits from which the believer benefits, and the unbeliever, and the dumb animal, and others. And among them are locks against evil, who close doors in which there is harm that destroys tillage and progeny and does away with kinds of living beings, whether animal or plant. And among them is the opposite of that: those who are locks against good, who find a broad door from which people live and then commit a sin by which that door disappears. How many a people whose affairs were upright and whose lives were good, and then the people of sins came and sinned and were extravagant, and God closed the door of that good from which they were living. You read in Sūrat Sabaʾ the story of the people of Sabaʾ, for whom God opened kinds of provision in this earth and made easy for them the ways of benefiting from them and made travel light for them and made the roads easy for them; but they transgressed and were tyrannical, so God changed that and destroyed them at the hands of the weakest of God's creatures, at the hands of a mouse. So God destroyed them by that and scattered them like the dispersal of Sabaʾ and made them a tale after having been a thing seen.

And likewise is the case with the nations that were tyrannical in all the lands. ʿAd, for whom God spread out kinds of provision and whom He increased in stature of body over the people of Noah and whose lives He lengthened — even so, when they transgressed and were tyrannical, God sent upon them the wind for eight successive days, and it did away with the green and the dry in their land. And their land to this day is such that no one can travel in it; and if a car travels in it and wants to turn back at the same hour, its track is lost and it cannot find its way to the place it came from. Their land today, the land of al-Ahqaf, is what is known as the Empty Quarter in the Arabian Peninsula; and the wind still continues in it, in the trace of that wind which God set loose for eight successive days. And likewise Thamud, for whom God made easy kinds of provision and made the mountains into houses: when they transgressed and were tyrannical, God sent upon them that blast which destroyed them and split the innermost of their hearts, so that not one of them could stand before it and they all perished in a single instant. And likewise the people of Lot and the other nations.

And those who lived at the point of balance of the world, in Mecca — may God ennoble and guard it — whenever they transgressed in the sanctuary, God would set over them what destroyed them and wiped them out. When God Most High made ready for Abraham the place of the House, and God appointed for Abraham the place of the House and commanded him to settle his household and his child beside it and showed him its place, God brought forth in this desolate valley in which there is no sowing — {in a valley without cultivation} (Sūrat Ibrāhīm 14:37) — this good water which has not ceased to this day of ours to give drink to the greatest of pilgrim assemblies, namely the water of Zamzam. The Amalekites dwelt with Hagar in that place, but when they transgressed in it, God set over them Jurhum, who killed them as ʿAd and Iram were killed and drove them out of it. Then when Jurhum transgressed, God destroyed them also and set over them those who came from the dam of Maʾrib, such as Khuzaʿah and others. Then when Khuzaʿah transgressed in the sanctuary, God set over them Qusayy and he drove them out. And that continued throughout the time of the age of ignorance. That is why a woman of Quraysh says to her son:

*My son, do not wrong in Mecca, neither the great nor the small.*

*My son, I have tried it, and found that whoever wrongs in it comes to ruin.*

*God made it safe, while no palaces were built in its precincts.*

*Tubbaʿ campaigned against it, and clothed its edifice in silk,*

*walking to it barefoot, with a thousand camels in its courtyard.*

*And God made its birds safe, and the mountain goats are safe on Thabir.*

Then, when Islam came — and the rule in the age of ignorance, and the restraint, had been by way of an inward force — Islam came and the perceptible, actual force appeared, and so that punishment was lifted, as Ibn ʿAbbas said. He said: the punishment that used to come upon the people of the age of ignorance in their ignorance was an inward punishment; and when the outward punishment came by the law of God, mighty and majestic, God lifted the inward punishment. In the age of ignorance a wolf would chase a hare until it entered the sanctuary, and then it would turn back and leave it; and today people have come to dare to commit acts of disobedience to God within His sanctuary, and to kill and to commit kinds of crimes, and they do not see some of those signs which the people of the age of ignorance used to see — and that is because God restrained by this religion and by what He laid down in His clear Book of the kinds of deterrents that suffice the people of faith and turn them back from tyranny.

An objective view of this economy requires moderation in dealing with this wealth. If a person looks at it knowing that he has no independence from it and that it is the nerve of life, but that it is not his property and that he will attain from it no more than his provision, then he will try to keep it in his hand and not to put it in his heart. For the resting-place of wealth in the Islamic view is the hand, and its resting-place in the other views is the heart. That is why the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "Wealth is not in the abundance of goods; wealth is rather the wealth of the soul." So you find the poor man who owns neither a dinar nor a dirham wealthy, at ease, content with what he has been given, disposing according to what God has given him: {God does not burden a soul beyond what He has given it} (Sūrat al-Ṭalāq 65:7). And you find the one who is rich in wealth, if the wealth is in his heart, that if he loses a single dirham of it the earth becomes straitened for him for all its breadth; and he is distracted from himself in the flood of increasing his wealth, until he becomes a servant of the world after it ought to have been the world that served him. Many people are worshippers of the world, serving it, while the world does not serve them: if God places some of this world under their hands it is a harm to them and a punishment and a burden, for they work for it night and day and spend their precious hours in serving it. And over against that we find others to whom He has given only a little of it, but who have used it to serve themselves, so that they have sent it ahead for their hereafter and sought help by it and kept themselves from need by it in their world; and by that they have made it easy in the correct easing, and have directed it according to what God has commanded. Hence their answer on the Day of Resurrection was a saving answer, and the answer of the former a disgracing one. For it is established from the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) that he said: "The two feet of a servant will not move on the Day of Resurrection until he is asked about four things: about his youth, in what he wore it out; and about his lifetime, in what he spent it; and about his wealth, from where he earned it and in what he spent it; and about his knowledge, what he did with it."

So about wealth he is asked two questions on the Day of Resurrection: from where did you earn it, and in what did you spend it? From where did you earn it — first, did you take it from what was lawful? And then after that, in what did you spend it — did you put it in its proper place? These two questions a person must keep before his eyes as he goes forth, and so sells his own soul and either frees it or destroys it. He knows that all people are traders, and that all of them are made by nature to love wealth; but their difference in that is that among them is one who takes it only from what is lawful and puts it only in its proper place, and is not tyrannical when it becomes abundant with him, and does not despair over what has escaped him of it — as He said, exalted is He: {so that you may not grieve over what has escaped you, nor rejoice over what He has given you} (Sūrat al-Ḥadīd 57:23). A person should not grieve over what has escaped him of it, because that is negative and makes him regretful and cut to pieces with regrets over a matter that is not within his power and that he cannot attain, so that it takes up part of his time and his thinking without benefiting him in anything. Nor is it for him to rejoice over what he has attained of it, because that is a cause of tyranny.

That is why the people of Qarun were giving good counsel when they said to him: {And seek, by means of what God has given you, the abode of the hereafter; and do not forget your share of this world; and do good as God has done good to you; and do not seek corruption in the earth. Indeed God does not love the corrupters} (Sūrat al-Qaṣaṣ 28:77). This is a complete law comprising four articles which everyone who strives to amass wealth ought to keep before his eyes. First, that he seek, in what God has given him, the abode of the hereafter. Second, that he not forget his share of this world and his portion of it. Third, that he do good as God has done good to him, and be conscious of his responsibility towards the poor when God has enriched him. Fourth — the fourth article — "and do not seek corruption in the earth": that he not seek corruption in the earth. If we tried to explain this, the discussion would run long with us, and we would bring only a few of the realities of the meaning of this verse, which is few in its words and many in its meanings.

For His words {And seek, in what God has given you, the abode of the hereafter} — He did not say in it: and seek, by all that God has given you, the abode of the hereafter, because that is a very lofty level of faith, namely that a person should give out everything he has in the path of God; and this only the truthful ones attain, and it cannot be a general law for all people. Rather He said: "and seek, in what God has given you, the abode of the hereafter" — and fī is for containment, which entails the middle course; for containment entails the middle. So he is not required to spend the best of his wealth, nor is he required to aim at the lowest of it: {And do not aim at the bad of it to spend, when you yourselves would not take it except with closed eyes} (Sūrat al-Baqarah 2:267). "In what God has given you" — the middle course. "In what God has given you, the abode of the hereafter; and do not forget your share of this world." This also requires of a person that he know that he has a small, limited share in this world: even if he lived a long life, when he is placed in his grave for the first time he forgets that whole lifetime and supposes that he lived in it only a day or two: {when the most exemplary of them in conduct will say: you stayed only a day} (Sūrat Ṭāhā 20:104). For this reason a person must know his portion of this world and know that it is not for him alone, and that it is for him to set it right and leave it to those who come after him. He is in the position of a rider who shelters in the shade of a tree: he ought not to cut it down nor to spoil it when his purpose in it is ended; rather he leaves it for whoever will shelter, and if he himself returns another time he will benefit from it.

And this prophetic similitude is very remarkable too, for the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) struck the similitude for us and said: "What have I to do with this world? I am only like a rider who took shade under a tree." When the rider sees trees he ought to choose the best of them and the fullest in shade and the cleanest in place, because he chooses for himself the suitable, fitting place; but for all that he does not weary himself greatly in improving this shade nor in settling in it, for he knows that the shade will shift. Quickly the shade shifts and turns and the shadow returns to the east; then the sun sets and at that point the shade vanishes: {then We made the sun an indicator over it; then We drew it in to Us with an easy drawing-in} (Sūrat al-Furqān 25:45–46) — this remarkable easy drawing-in. Likewise, if a rider shelters in the shade of a tree, that often makes it a place of permanent shade for whoever comes after him, because the Arabs say:

*And you will never chance upon a fertile pasture but that you find in it the traces of one who came there to graze.*

So the place in which people habitually take shade will be frequented and people will take shade in it, and if a caravan departs from it another returns to it. Likewise it is among the things by which people find the landmarks of the earth; and it has come in the hadith that whoever alters the landmarks of the earth is cursed. What is meant by that is that whoever cuts down the trees that are landmarks in the earth, or alters the roads and the ways, leads by that act of his to destruction and corruption in the earth, and he is cursed on the tongue of Muhammad (peace and blessings be upon him).

After this He said: {And do good as God has done good to you}. The rich must be conscious that God, mighty and majestic, is the one who apportioned these provisions, and that He did not apportion them on the basis of intelligence, nor on the basis of knowledge, nor on the basis of standing, nor on the basis of bodily strength; rather He apportioned them for a wisdom and made them an examination and a responsibility. So whoever God has given this wealth has a great responsibility towards the poor. He must be conscious that he is a father to a group of people whose provisions God has placed under his hand and over whom He has given him charge and made him steward of their provisions. He is one of the ways of good and one of its roads: either he takes much of it or he takes little. For this reason, those under whose hands God has placed people's provisions, if they do good, attain the rewards of everyone who benefits from the wealth under their hands; and if they do ill, there will be written against them the burdens of those whom they denied what they deserved and from whom they barred what God created for them.

This sets out a great principle of the Sharia under which many rules ought to enter. For its sake God forbade usurious gain (ribā); and for its sake God forbade cornering the market; and for its sake God forbade extravagance; and for its sake God forbade cheating and betrayal; and for its sake God, glorified and exalted, forbade unacceptable uncertainty in a sale; and for its sake God, glorified and exalted, forbade destruction of property and the breaking of minted coin, and other kinds of corruption in the earth. These foundations were forbidden only for the sake of the responsibility that lies upon the rich towards the poor. And if they become conscious of it, they will improve wealth not for themselves but so as to be spenders

upon a great number of people, and so that mutual support may increase thereby among people.

For this reason God, glorified and exalted, laid down zakat upon wealth and made it obligatory (wājib) upon the rich, to be taken from their rich and returned to their poor; and it is a right in the wealth itself. And He laid down other rights in wealth as well, for in wealth there is a right other than zakat, as the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) stated explicitly. Among those rights he mentioned that a person should milk from the udders of his livestock when he brings them to water and finds those in need of that at the watering-places. Likewise among these rights are the outlays from the crop when its ripeness appears, as in His words, exalted is He: {And give its due on the day of its harvest, and do not be extravagant; indeed He does not love the extravagant} (Sūrat al-Anʿām 6:141) — "and give its due on the day of its harvest". This right which is obligatory on the day of the harvest, most of the exegetes have said, is other than the obligatory zakat, because zakat is not obligatory on the day of the harvest specifically; it is rather a right additional to it, and it is the charity of thanksgiving for what God has brought forth for us of fruits.

Likewise the laying down of the other voluntary charities, and the unrestricted social solidarity by which the connection between human beings is completed and the bonds between them are tied — such as the bridal gift (mahr) between a man and a woman, and the obligatory maintenance between a parent and his child, and a husband and his wife, and an owned person and his owner: all these outlays enter into the framework of this social solidarity, which is part of financial responsibility.

Likewise the general right in wealth: for in wealth there is a general right belonging to the whole community, taken either by way of voluntary giving or by way of assessment and estimation. The community has reached consensus that it is not lawful to take taxes from people without their consent, and that this is only in a case of necessity. The first time this community knew taxes was in the days of al-Muttaqi the Abbasid, at the beginning of the fourth century of the Hijrah, in the year three hundred and ten; and the scholars condemned that. Al-Qarafi, may God have mercy on him, stated explicitly that whoever holds taxes to be permissible has disbelieved in God the Almighty. What he means by that is that the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) went to great lengths in forbidding the taking of wealth without willingness of soul, for he said: "Indeed your blood and your property and your honour are inviolable to you, like the inviolability of this day of yours, in this month of yours, in this land of yours" — and this entails the basic inviolability. But for all that, al-ʿIzz ibn ʿAbd al-Salam and others stated explicitly that if the public treasury needs what will meet the general needs of the people, then that need is examined and assessed and estimated, and then its measure is not exceeded; and people are asked to give voluntarily. If they give voluntarily what meets that, well and good; and if they do not give that voluntarily, it is taken from them — but he begins with the class of the great rich and then those next to them, so that it may be by a just apportionment.

Hence taxes were in fact developed by the Westerners; it is they who imposed them and made them a source among the sources of the public treasury and an item among the items of the budgets upon which states rest. Their method in them differs from the method of the countries of the Third World. The Westerners' method in taxes is that taxes do not enter the general treasury, but enter designated funds: so if a tax is taken from people for roads, it is put in a fund designated for repairing roads, and whoever's road to his house has not been repaired — the law gives him the right to refuse to pay the tax until the road to his house is repaired for him. And likewise the taxes taken for building schools have a designated fund; and likewise the taxes taken for building hospitals have a designated fund; and likewise the taxes taken for social pensions and for what the municipalities pay to the poor who live in their jurisdiction — all of that has designated funds. But in the Third World the taxes are paid to the general treasury of the state, and are mixed with all its properties; and hence they become a thing circulating among the rich, and the people of authority take them and no one else benefits from them, and they depart from the purpose for which they were brought out and for which they were laid down. Hence they become a burden, so that people's souls are not content to pay them out, because they see nothing accomplished by them; and they evade them with kinds of evasion, so that only a small part of them is brought in. For that reason the regimes standing in the countries of the Third World admit their complete inability to collect the prescribed taxes. And that is due to two things: first, that these taxes are unjust and not in accordance with the law of God; second, that these taxes are likewise not convincing to people, because they have not been spent on what convinces people and satisfies them, but are spent into the pockets of people who do not deserve them.

Likewise, among the sources of social solidarity and among its required aspects is what the Lawgiver has set out, that the rich must participate with their wealth in raising high the word of God Most High and in strengthening His religion. This includes their spending on striving in the path of God and campaigning against the enemy, and their spending likewise on the learning of knowledge and on the communal obligations, and on the building of bridges and mosques and hospitals, and other kinds of public benefits that people need. In the earliest period of Islam these things were established as individual projects undertaken by particular individuals: they would establish schools of their own accord and make them endowments (awqāf) and endow shops and farms upon them, and that guaranteed their permanence and their continuance and their freedom. For this reason they brought forth the great, eminent scholars, because they lived in an atmosphere of freedom that guaranteed their continuance and non-interference in their decisions. But when the endowments of the schools were taken and they became institutions belonging to states, they lived in the embrace of servitude and lost the breath of freedom; and for this reason they did not bring forth scholars, but became one of the corrupt institutions of the system.

Notice that al-Azhar was a free institution, spent upon from the endowments which the merchants of the Muslims endowed upon it over long centuries. It brought forth a great number of scholars and the community of Muhammad (peace and blessings be upon him) benefited from it across the centuries. But its endowments were nationalised and taken for the benefit of the state, and al-Azhar came to be spent upon from the budget of the state, and the state became the one that appoints and dismisses in it and lays down for it the curricula and the programmes. So its role stopped and its giving stopped, and it no longer brought forth what it used to bring forth of scholars. And likewise in the various other countries.

Then the hospitals too — individuals and merchants used to build them and give them voluntarily for the benefit of the community, and endow upon them endowments with continuing revenue, so that the community benefited from that; and this continued for a long time in the community of Muhammad (peace and blessings be upon him), and people lived well by it — until their nationalisation took place and they reverted to institutions owned by the public sector, behind which there is neither care nor maintenance, and for which no designated funds are allocated; or else they became properties of the private sector, a field for competition, not directed by the spirit of humanity and solidarity, so that they became a place for earning money and competing in amassing it, and the original motive of solidarity was no longer in them. In former times a man would exert himself to build a mosque and to set up a school and to found a māristān — and the māristān is the hospital. Concerning that one of the poets says, in praise of one of the scholars: *You founded a school and a māristān, to set right religions and bodies.*

So the school is for setting right religions and the māristān for setting right bodies. Likewise among the aspects of this solidarity are the blood-monies paid by the ʿāqilah. For error is not of a person's earning and it is not within his capacity to escape it; and were it laid upon him, his production would be diminished and his thoughts would fall short of what he produces for the benefit of this community. If a person who drives his car and has an accident without intending it, in which a number of people die, were charged with the blood-monies of all of them, people would give up driving cars and many beneficial projects would come to a halt. And likewise if a person knew that if he built a building and it collapsed during its construction without his intending it, he would pay the blood-monies of those affected by it, people would stop building and many benefits for humanity would be suspended. And likewise in digging, and likewise in extracting minerals, and likewise in the other kinds of beneficial projects. So God Most High made, as an encouragement to people in this, these ʿāqilahs which take on the error on behalf of those responsible for it and bear the blood-monies for error, whether that be in lives or in faculties or in bones and head-wounds.

Likewise the registers (dawāwīn) which stand in the place of the ʿāqilahs. For urban civilisation is contrary to tribalism, which is in origin a bedouin system; and in urban civilisation the tribes come together and the lineages mix and tribal partisanship becomes light. For this reason a substitute for the ʿāqilahs was needed in it, and so ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, established, by the consensus of the Companions, the registers, in which the members of each profession came to pay the blood-money in solidarity among themselves. So the police pay blood-money one for another, and the army pay one for another, and the teachers pay one for another, and the doctors pay one for another, and so on. This is when the tribal system disappears and urban civilisation mixes and partisan loyalties fall away.

These aspects of solidarity and complementarity among humanity ought not to be neglected, and ought to be supported and strengthened in the life of humanity, so that it may be known from where this wealth is brought and in what it is spent.

Then a person must not be extravagant. That is why He said: {And do good as God has done good to you, and do not seek corruption in the earth}. For corruption in the earth takes in extravagance in expenditure, because a person has a capacity and has a need; so he must bring his need close to what he draws upon, for what he needs ought not to be more than what he produces. And if he produces much, then he must not increase that in his requirements, and must direct those requirements rightly, because among humanity are a people who do not produce at all and he stands over them in exchange for that. Hence God, glorified and exalted, informed us of Himself that He does not love the extravagant. That is why Muhammad Mawlud ibn Ahmad Fal, may God Most High have mercy on him, says:

*Extravagance! Extravagance! Indeed extravagance — God Most High has forbidden it, and that is enough.*

*"And He does not love the extravagant" is enough to restrain your hand from extravagance.*

The scholars have differed over extravagance, whether it enters into acts of piety or not; and they have agreed that it enters into all worldly matters. A group of them held that extravagance enters even into acts of piety: so the man who gives all his wealth in charity, if he knows his own need of it and has no arrangement by which he will be compensated, is extravagant. They argued for this by the fact that the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him), when it reached him that Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas had harvested his palms and given away all their fruit in charity and had not kept back a single date to break his fast with, became very angry about that. This is evidence that extravagance in such matters is not praiseworthy in the Sharia. So a person must leave what he will spend on his family.

It is established in the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from the hadith of Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas, may God be pleased with him, that he fell ill in Mecca and the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) came to visit him, and he said: Messenger of God, I am a man of wealth and only a little daughter of mine will inherit from me. Shall I give all my wealth in charity in the path of God? He said: No. Hold back some of your wealth for yourself. He said: Shall I give two-thirds of it in charity? He said: No. He said: Shall I give half of it in charity? He said: No. He said: Shall I give a third of it in charity? He said: Yes, and a third is much. That you leave your heirs wealthy is better than that you leave them destitute, begging from people. And you are soon to be left behind, so that peoples will benefit by you and others will be harmed by you. I said: Messenger of God, shall I be left behind after my companions? He said: Yes; you will not spend an expenditure by which you seek the face of God but that you are rewarded for it, even what you place in your wife's mouth. So Saʿd lived after this for a time, and twelve children of his own loins inherited from him, and he gave out a third of his wealth in the path of God several times after that.

This requires of us that we not be hasty in our view and that our view be balanced. God Most High has given a person a third of his wealth which he may bequeath, even in the state of his final illness: "God has given you a third of your wealth at the end of your lives, for you to give in charity" — and this is the bequest. And the bequest does not exceed a third; so it is not permissible for a person to bequeath more than a third of his wealth.

Then extravagance likewise takes in harmful extravagance, namely extravagance in food and drink and the like, which entails harm to the body. And this harm is of kinds: for there is nothing in which there is a benefit but that in it is another kind of harm. Water has benefits beyond counting, and yet in it are harms, for it entails a reduction in some of the secretions of the stomach which a person needs in digesting his food. And likewise the other kinds of things tasted and the kinds of things a person uses on himself: if they exceed the need or are taken alone and unmixed, they harm. Hence many of the diseases known today have their cause in food: such as diabetes, which arises from extravagance in starches; and heart disease, which arises from extravagance in fats; and kidney disease, which likewise arises from extravagance in foods and shortage of drink. And likewise the other kinds of diseases, such as some skin diseases, which arise from extravagance in the use of sugar, such as vitiligo and tinea and others. And likewise some diseases arise from extravagance in the use of salts, and some arise from extravagance in the use of liquids, and so on. Among them is flabbiness, which is excess obesity, for it arises from the use of liquids and extravagance in them beyond the need, since it entails an expansion in the belly, and that entails a keenness for foods; so when a person eats much and is extravagant in them his body swells, and that is one of the diseases, because it weakens his faculties and leads to friction in his joints and to the stopping of the places of growth in his body, and often leads to many diseases.

And likewise movements: extravagance in them entails certain diseases. Extravagance in sports entails disease in the cartilage that lies between the vertebrae of the back, so that it is stretched and extended; and likewise extravagance in walking entails diseases in the knees, such as friction and congestion and the like. So extravagance is a harm, whatever this extravagance may be. And likewise extravagance in clothing entails harm too, for the increase of their weight is a weight upon a person and an added weight upon his own weight; and a person has a limited capacity and must not increase his weight beyond it and must not let his permanent load increase beyond it. Hence many diseases arise from lack of evenness in the two sandals: if wear occurs in the sandal, a person will walk unevenly, one of his legs higher than the other, and he is afflicted with disease and a deficiency of balance because of that, since the speed of the blood in one of the two sides will be greater than its speed in the other side; and this often leads to some cancers, and especially cancer in the blood and others. Hence one of the companies that used to manufacture sandals in the United States of America had a case brought against it in the courts because its sandals were not carefully weighted in point of size; a case was brought against it and this led to its bankruptcy and the taking of its wealth.

So this requires of us the avoidance of extravagance absolutely. And the scholars mention that extravagance in reading likewise entails bodily diseases and an increase in the mental faculty. The mental faculty and the other faculties God has weighed according to a person's body and according to his spirit; so if they increase, his balance is disturbed. Many people want an increase of intellect and wish for that, but do not know that if his intellect were increased it would entail a disturbance in him, because God weighed him upon this balance and determined him by this determining. That is why God, glorified and exalted, says: {Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High, who created and proportioned} (Sūrat al-Aʿlā 87:1–2). This remarkable determining is entailed by the wisdom of God, glorified and exalted, and it is the remarkable evenness in the creation of the human being: the two forearms must be of one size, and the two hands of one size, and the two ears likewise, and the two eyes likewise, and the two legs and the two shins and the two thighs, and so on, until the human being's frame is complete. And whatever departs from this is a defect in the creation and a deficiency in it and a weakness in the human constitution.

flags.arabic: وقد صرح القرافي رحمه الله بأن من قال بجواز الضرائب فقد كفر بالله العظيم، ويقصد بذلك أن الرسول (ص) بالغ في تحريم أخذ المال من غير طيبوبة النفس … ولكن مع ذلك نص العز بن عبد السلام وغيره على أنه إذا احتاج بيت المال …

flags.note: CRITICAL FOR DISPLAY AND EDITORIAL REVIEW (house rules 6, 10 and 12). This passage contains a statement of unbelief — al-Qarafi's, that whoever holds taxation permissible has disbelieved in God — quoted by the Sheikh. Three things must travel with it and are preserved in the English. (a) The attribution: it is al-Qarafi's statement, not the Sheikh's. (b) The Sheikh's own immediate gloss, 'what he means by that is…', which reduces it to an emphatic statement of the inviolability of property, not a takfīr ruling on tax authorities. (c) Al-ʿIzz ibn ʿAbd al-Salam's position, given straight after, that the treasury may assess and levy what public need requires when voluntary giving falls short, beginning with the wealthiest. Quoted alone, the first sentence is a takfīr of every modern government and every citizen who accepts taxation. The site must not allow it to be excerpted alone, and the record should carry a display rule to that effect. Nothing has been softened: the Sheikh does state the consensus that taxes without consent are unlawful except under necessity.

Strip them from body_ar as well

flags.arabic: وأول ما عرفت هذه الأمة الضرائب كان في أيام المتقي العباسي في القرن الرابع الهجري في بدايته بسنة ثلاثمائة وعشر
flags.context: The historical claim about the first appearance of taxation.
options: Translate the date as the source gives it and flag the discrepancy
Correct the year to al-Muttaqi's reign
flags.note: SOURCE DEFECT (house rule 11). The Sheikh dates the first taxation to the days of al-Muttaqi the Abbasid, 'at the beginning of the fourth century of the Hijrah, in the year three hundred and ten'. Al-Muttaqi's caliphate was 329–333 AH; 310 AH falls in the reign of al-Muqtadir. Either the year or the caliph's name is wrong in the record. Both have been rendered exactly as given and neither has been corrected.

flags.arabic: «دخلت امرأة النار في هرة ربطتها، لا هي أطعمتها ولا هي أرسلتها تأكل من خشاش الأرض، فهذا يقتضي … / «فإن دماءكم وأموالكم وأعراضكم عليكم حرام كحرمة يومكم هذا في شهركم هذا في بلدكم هذا، وهذا مقتض لأصل الحرمة
flags.context: Two hadith quotations in the record.
options: Close the quotation where the hadith ends and flag the missing marker
Extend the quotation to where the source's guillemet would have closed
flags.note: SOURCE DEFECT (house rule 11). In both cases the CMS text opens a quotation with a guillemet and never closes it, so that the Sheikh's own commentary runs on inside the quotation marks. The English closes each quotation where the hadith text demonstrably ends — after 'from the creatures of the earth' and after 'in this land of yours' — and this judgement is recorded here rather than made silently. A reviewer should confirm the boundary against the recording.

flags.arabic: وآتوا حقه يوم حصاه / وهو يغدوا فبائع نفسه / فلا يستورد منها إلا جزء قليل / وهو صدق الشكر على ما أخرج الله لنا من الثمرات
flags.context: Four word-level defects in the second half of the record.
options: Preserve each in body_ar and render the evident sense in body_en
Flag them as uncertain in the English
flags.note: SOURCE DEFECT (house rule 11). 'حصاه' is truncated from 'حصاده' — the Qur'anic wording is given correctly two words earlier in the same sentence, so this is a transcription slip. 'يغدوا' is an orthographic error for 'يغدو'. 'يستورد' appears to be an error for 'يورد' (is brought in), and is rendered by that sense. 'صدق الشكر' is most likely 'صدقة الشكر', the charity of thanksgiving, and is rendered so; the reading is not certain and a reviewer should check it.

flags.arabic: فكثير من الأمراض المعروفة اليوم سببها في الغذاء، كالمرض السكري فهو ناشئ عن الإسراف في النشويات … فيؤدي هذا كثيرا إلى بعض السرطانات وبالأخص السرطان في الدم … أقيمت عليها دعوى في المحاكم بسبب أن نعالها لم تكن مبالغا في وزنها
flags.context: The closing section on extravagance and the body.
options: Publish with an explicit note that these are not medical statements
flags.note: EDITORIAL REVIEW REQUIRED (house rule 12). The final section makes a run of specific aetiological claims — diabetes from starches, heart disease from fats, kidney disease from food and too little drink, vitiligo from sugar, blood cancer from unevenly worn sandals — and reports an American footwear company bankrupted by litigation over shoe weight. These are the Sheikh's illustrations of the Qur'anic prohibition of extravagance, not clinical teaching, and they have been translated faithfully without hedging or strengthening. But in English on a public site they read as medical claims and are capable of causing harm. The site should carry a clear statement that they are not medical advice, and the shoe-company anecdote, which names no company and cites no source, should not be presented as established fact.

flags.arabic: أما حين أخذت أوقاف المدارس وأصبحت مؤسسات تابعة للدول فإنها عاشت في أحضان العبودية … وإنما أصبحت مؤسسة من مؤسسات النظام الفاسدة، لاحظوا أن الأزهر كان مؤسسة حرة
flags.context: The passage on endowments and the nationalisation of religious institutions.
flags.note: EDITORIAL REVIEW (house rule 12). The Sheikh states that state-run religious institutions 'live in the embrace of servitude' and have become 'corrupt institutions of the system', and names al-Azhar as the example, attributing the end of its scholarly productivity to the nationalisation of its endowments. This is a direct criticism of a named, still existing institution and of the Egyptian state's handling of it. It has been translated exactly. Note that his argument is structural — about the independence that endowment funding gives — and not about the persons of its scholars; the English preserves that distinction and does not sharpen it.

flags.arabic: أبني لا تظلم بمـ ** ـكة لا الكبير ولا الصغير … / أنشأت مدرسة ومارستانا** لتصحح الأديان والأبدانا / ولن تصادف مرعى ممرعا أبدا** إلا وجدت به آثار منتجع / والسرفَ السرفَ إن السرفا** عنه نهى الله تعالى وكفى
flags.context: The poetry quoted through the lecture.
options: Translate as prose in italics and record the source's markup in the flag
flags.note: FORMATTING NOTE (style guide §4). The CMS marks hemistich boundaries with a doubled asterisk; in the first line of the Qurashi woman's poem the word 'بمكة' is itself split across the boundary ('بمـ ** ـكة'), which is how the Arabic scribal convention handles a word broken at the end of a hemistich. That markup is preserved in body_ar and does not appear in body_en. All four passages are given as prose in italics and no rhymed English has been attempted. The verse of Muhammad Mawlud is a didactic nazm and its second line quotes the Qur'anic phrase inside the verse; the English keeps the quotation visible.

flags.arabic: إن من تدبيره سبحانه وتعالى أن أمم هذه الأرزاق في هذه الأرض ولم يجعلها ملكا فرديا لمكتشفها
flags.context: The transition to the section on wealth as God's property.
flags.note: UNCERTAIN. The verb 'أمّم' in modern Arabic means 'nationalised', and the Sheikh uses it in exactly that modern sense later in the same lecture, of the endowments of al-Azhar. Used here of God's arrangement it must mean something closer to 'made them common property, not the finder's'. The English renders it that way, which the following clause supports; but the deliberate echo between the two uses — God made wealth common, states made endowments theirs — may be part of the Sheikh's rhetoric and is recorded here so that a reviewer can decide whether to preserve it in English.

translator_notes: Qur'anic renderings in this file are interpretive translations of meaning, offered to carry the Sheikh's argument in English. They are not a substitute for the Arabic text of the Qur'an.

This is the first part of a lecture on social justice; the second part is article 457, which begins mid-sentence and continues directly from the closing discussion of extravagance here. The two records should be displayed as a pair.

The three-tier scheme of ḍarūriyyāt, ḥājiyyāt and taḥsīniyyāt — necessities, needs and refinements — is the organising structure of the first half. The Sheikh also uses takmīliyyāt as a synonym for taḥsīniyyāt, and the English renders it 'complements' to keep the two words distinct as he does.
Qur'anic quotations in this record are given in the Arabic with full vowelling, unlike most records in this corpus, which give them unvowelled. body_ar preserves the vowelling exactly.

Hadith attributions are kept as the Sheikh gives them — 'established in the two Ṣaḥīḥs', 'established from the Messenger of God' — and no grading or collection has been added where he gives none, as with the hadith on the curse upon one who alters the landmarks of the earth and the report on the third of one's wealth.

The ruling terms are rendered strictly: 'واجبة' is 'obligatory (wājib)'; 'لا يجوز' is 'not permissible'; 'لا يحل' is 'not lawful'; 'حرم الله' is 'God forbade'. 'الربا' is 'usurious gain (ribā)' and 'الجهالة في البيع' is 'unacceptable uncertainty in a sale' (gharar), per the glossary.

'العواقل' is rendered 'the ʿāqilahs' — the kin-groups that bear blood-money for unintentional harm — and 'الدواوين' 'the registers', with the Sheikh's own explanation of each left to do the defining, rather than substituting a modern term such as 'insurance pool' which he does not use.
'مارستان' is kept in transliteration with the Sheikh's own gloss ('and the māristān is the hospital'), because the poetry he quotes turns on the word.
